In [[mathematics]], the '''Minkowski–Steiner formula''' is a formula relating the [[area|surface area]] and [[volume]] of [[compact space|compact]] [[subset]]s of [[Euclidean space]]. More precisely, it defines the surface area as the "derivative" of enclosed volume in an appropriate sense.

The Minkowski–Steiner formula is used, together with the [[Brunn–Minkowski theorem]], to prove the [[isoperimetric inequality]]. It is named after [[Hermann Minkowski]] and [[Jakob Steiner]].

==Statement of the Minkowski-Steiner formula==

Let <math>n \geq 2</math>, and let <math>A \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be a compact set. Let <math>\mu (A)</math> denote the [[Lebesgue measure]] (volume) of <math>A</math>. Define the quantity <math>\lambda (\partial A)</math> by the '''Minkowski–Steiner formula'''

:<math>\lambda (\partial A) := \liminf_{\delta \to 0} \frac{\mu \left( A + \overline{B_{\delta}} \right) - \mu (A)}{\delta},</math>

where

:<math>\overline{B_{\delta}} := \left\{ x = (x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \left| | x | := \sqrt{x_{1}^{2} + \dots + x_{n}^{2}} \leq \delta \right. \right\}</math>

denotes the [[closed ball]] of [[radius]] <math>\delta > 0</math>, and

:<math>A + \overline{B_{\delta}} := \left\{ a + b \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \left| a \in A, b \in \overline{B_{\delta}} \right. \right\}</math>

is the [[Minkowski sum]] of <math>A</math> and <math>\overline{B_{\delta}}</math>, so that

:<math>A + \overline{B_{\delta}} = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathrel|\ \mathopen| x - a \mathclose| \leq \delta \mbox{ for some } a \in A \right\}.</math>

==Remarks==

===Surface measure===

For "sufficiently regular" sets <math>A</math>, the quantity <math>\lambda (\partial A)</math> does indeed correspond with the <math>(n - 1)</math>-dimensional measure of the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] <math>\partial A</math> of <math>A</math>. See Federer (1969) for a full treatment of this problem.

===Convex sets===

When the set <math>A</math> is a [[convex set]], the [[limit inferior|lim-inf]] above is a true [[Limit of a sequence|limit]], and one can show that

:<math>\mu \left( A + \overline{B_{\delta}} \right) = \mu (A) + \lambda (\partial A) \delta + \sum_{i = 2}^{n - 1} \lambda_{i} (A) \delta^{i} + \omega_{n} \delta^{n},</math>

where the <math>\lambda_{i}</math> are some [[continuous function]]s of <math>A</math> (see [[quermassintegral]]s) and <math>\omega_{n}</math> denotes the measure (volume) of the [[unit ball]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>:

:<math>\omega_{n} = \frac{2 \pi^{n / 2}}{n \Gamma (n / 2)},</math>

where <math>\Gamma</math> denotes the [[Gamma function]].

==Example: volume and surface area of a ball==

Taking <math>A = \overline{B_{R}}</math> gives the following well-known formula for the surface area of the [[sphere]] of radius <math>R</math>, <math>S_{R} := \partial B_{R}</math>:

:<math>\lambda (S_{R}) = \lim_{\delta \to 0} \frac{\mu \left( \overline{B_{R}} + \overline{B_{\delta}} \right) - \mu \left( \overline{B_{R}} \right)}{\delta}</math>
::<math>= \lim_{\delta \to 0} \frac{[ (R + \delta)^{n} - R^{n} ] \omega_{n}}{\delta}</math>
::<math>= n R^{n - 1} \omega_{n},</math>

where <math>\omega_{n}</math> is as above.
